documents: Druzhbin et al. (2022) Water enhancement of Si self-diffusion in wadsleyite, JGR Solid Earth 127, e2021JB023440 (published PDF, 13 pages)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (identical to the printed 'n of 13' pages)

entry.evidence: Thus, the magnitude of H2O effect on wadsleyite rheology is still unknown.

steps.action: Cite Hustoft et al. (2013) deformation experiments showing H2O weakening of wadsleyite and ringwoodite, with poorly controlled H2O contents.
steps.quote: Although Hustoft et al. (2013) observed H2O weakening of wadsleyite and ringwoodite by deformation experiments

steps.action: Recall the authors' earlier dislocation-recovery estimate of an H2O-content exponent of 1.1 for dislocation mobility in ringwoodite.
steps.quote: By this technique, a H2O content exponent of 1.1 ± 0.1 was obtained for the dislocation mobility in ringwoodite.

steps.action: Cite Shimojuku et al. Si diffusion coefficients in polycrystalline wadsleyite over a narrow H2O range, which indicate weakening but give no exponent.
steps.quote: are about half an order of magnitude higher than those with 20–60 wt. ppm H2O

steps.action: Pose the open question of how large the H2O effect on wadsleyite rheology is, and whether Si diffusion is anisotropic.
steps.quote: Thus, the magnitude of H2O effect on wadsleyite rheology is still unknown.

steps.action: Design measurements on oriented single crystals over 10–5,300 wt. ppm H2O, along three axes, with NanoSIMS to reduce surface-roughness effects.
steps.quote: we systematically measured the Si self-diffusion coefficients in wadsleyite single crystals as a function of H2O content from 10 to 5,300 wt. ppm

steps.action: Synthesize Fe-free wadsleyite single crystals at 21 GPa and 2050 K, coat them with 29Si-enriched films, and anneal diffusion couples at 19–20 GPa and 1573–1873 K in sealed gold capsules.
steps.quote: annealed at 19–20 GPa and 1573–1873 K for 0–600 min.

steps.action: Measure 29Si/28Si depth profiles with NanoSIMS in 10 × 10 μm2 craters, use only the central 2.5 × 2.5 μm2 region, and convert time to depth from crater depths.
steps.quote: The diffusion profiles were measured using Cameca NanoSIMS 50 L installed at the Institute of Geology and Geophysics

steps.action: Fit the profiles with an error-function solution (Eq. 1) to obtain apparent Si diffusion coefficients.
steps.quote: The diffusion coefficients were obtained by fitting the diffusion profiles to the error function,

steps.action: Check the topography artifact: limit craters to smooth areas (topography under 60 nm) and run zero-time experiments, which give a linear L(σ) relation matching Fei et al. (2012).
steps.quote: The nominal diffusion lengths (L) in these runs were found to be a linear function of surface topography (σ)

steps.action: Correct the apparent diffusion coefficients for SIMS convolution, heating-up diffusion and topography using the zero-time L(σ) relation (Eq. 2).
steps.quote: where DSi is the Si diffusion coefficient after the correction.

steps.action: Measure H2O contents by unpolarized FTIR with the Beer-Lambert law (Bolfan-Casanova coefficient), and also give values corrected for orientation using the Jacobsen et al. (2005) polarization ratios.
steps.quote: The H2O content in each recovered sample was determined by unpolarized Fourier transformation infrared spectroscopy (FTIR)

steps.action: Check that H2O contents before and after annealing agree within a factor of 1.5, and argue from cited proton diffusivity that H2O equilibrates within 1 min.
steps.quote: the CH2O in the samples did not vary significantly, that is, within a factor of 1.5 (Table 1)

steps.action: Report that DSi rises about two orders of magnitude with H2O content and about 1.5 orders with temperature, with no detectable anisotropy.
steps.quote: DSi increases systematically by about two orders of magnitude with increasing CH2O from ∼10 to 5,300 wt. ppm

steps.action: Least-squares fit of an Arrhenius law with an H2O-content factor (Eq. 4), giving r = 0.8 ± 0.1, ΔH = 270 ± 40 kJ/mol and D0.
steps.quote: ΔH = 270 ± 40 kJ/mol, by assuming r independent from T.

steps.action: Refit r with H2O contents with and without the orientation correction (0.82 ± 0.12 vs 0.77 ± 0.11).
steps.quote: The fitting of r based on CH2O without and with orientation correction do not [...]

steps.action: Compare the exponent with Si diffusion in olivine (r = 0.32) and Mg diffusion in wadsleyite (r = 0.3).
steps.quote: which is a strong contrast to the Si diffusion in its low-pressure polymorph, olivine

steps.action: Compare with Shimojuku et al.: the temperature dependence is comparable, but the absolute DSi is higher than theirs.
steps.quote: However, the absolute values of DSi in this study are higher (Figure 7)

steps.action: Attribute the discrepancy to auxiliaries (polycrystals, topography, Si activity, temperature calibration) and argue that none of them affects the H2O exponent.
steps.quote: However, all of those causes should not affect the CH2O exponent for DSi determined in this study.

steps.action: Set out rival rate-limiting Si defect species and charge-neutrality conditions, within a vacancy-diffusion defect-chemistry frame, for wadsleyite, ringwoodite and olivine.
steps.quote: Below we discuss the defect chemistry of the three polymorphs individually to interpret the different CH2O exponents for DSi and DMg.

steps.action: Derive the fH2O exponents of each defect concentration under each charge-neutrality condition (Table 2).
steps.quote: The exponent values are calculated following Kohlstedt (2006).

steps.action: Compare the measured r = 0.8 with the Table 2 predictions: (2H)Si, VSi or HSi are compatible; (3H)Si and (4H)Si would give exponents of 3/2 or more.
steps.quote: The current CH2O exponent of r = 0.8 ± 0.1 for DSi in Fe-free wadsleyite suggests that Si diffusion is controlled

steps.action: Exclude VSi and HSi in Fe-bearing wadsleyite because they would predict negative H2O dependence, against the observed water weakening.
steps.quote: are excluded as the dominant species for Si diffusion in Fe-bearing wadsleyite

steps.action: Keep (2H)Si as the most likely Si diffusion species, assuming the same mechanism in Fe-free and Fe-bearing wadsleyite; infer (3H)Si for ringwoodite and VSi for olivine.
steps.quote: [...] assume the same Si diffusion mechanism in Fe-bearing and Fe-free wadsleyite, DSi is most likely controlled by migration of

steps.action: Keep the result that Si diffusion is nearly isotropic, attributing the apparent factor-of-three anisotropy to scatter, and explain it by Si escape from the SiO4 tetrahedron.
steps.quote: the DSi in wadsleyite is found to be isotropic under both H2O-poor and H2O-rich conditions

steps.action: Compute relative viscosity (η ∝ 1/DSi) across the transition zone for H2O-rich and H2O-poor wadsleyite, using r ≈ 1.1 for ringwoodite.
steps.quote: Therefore, the H2O incorporation dramatically reduces the viscosity of both wadsleyite and ringwoodite

steps.action: Cite seismic images of 60 plumes that narrow or broaden in the transition zone (Zhao 2007), whose cause is unknown.
steps.quote: Some plumes such as Iceland, Hainan, and Galapagos are accelerated and narrowed in the mantle transition zone

steps.action: Propose that the viscosity contrast between plume and surrounding transition zone, set by water and temperature, controls plume shape.
steps.quote: the viscosity contrast of wadsleyite (and ringwoodite) between the plumes and the surrounding mantle may provide an answer

steps.action: Compute plume versus transition-zone viscosity for ΔT = +200 or +500 K and 0.01 or 1.0 wt.% H2O (Figure 8).
steps.quote: the viscosity contrast between the plume and surrounding mantle in the transition zone can be evaluated with various temperature and H2O content conditions

steps.action: Compare the expected viscosity contrasts with the seismically imaged plume shapes, including the inverted-triangle shape of narrowed plumes near 410 km.
steps.quote: It explains the inverted-triangle-shape of the narrowed plumes such as Iceland, Galapagos, Hainan, and San Felix near the 410-km depth boundary

tree.answer: Water weakening of wadsleyite, reported earlier but not quantified
No; rheology is inferred from Si diffusion coefficients fitted to SIMS profiles
Estimate the H2O exponent, activation enthalpy and anisotropy of DSi
Rival rate-limiting Si defect species under different charge-neutrality conditions
Yes; distinct fH2O exponents for each species (Table 2)
Set in the laboratory: P, T and H2O content in multi-anvil runs
Yes, against zero-time controls, H2O stability checks and the orientation-correction choice

end.claim: Si self-diffusion in Fe-free wadsleyite is enhanced by H2O with a content exponent r = 0.8 ± 0.1 and activation enthalpy 270 ± 40 kJ/mol, implying strong H2O weakening of the transition zone.

decisive_move.sentence: The least-squares fit of Eq. 4 to topography-corrected DSi over a wide H2O range (10–5,300 wt. ppm) produces the exponent that earlier narrow-range work could not.

gates.evidence: The prior indication of water weakening (Shimojuku, Hustoft) motivated the systematic variation of H2O content, but the aim was to estimate a parameter rather than test a stated hypothesis. The exponent could have come out near zero, and the defect-species comparison against Table 2 could have failed. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Kröger-Vink point-defect chemistry and charge-neutrality analysis
Pulsed laser deposition of isotopically enriched thin films
Error-function solution of the diffusion equation
Thermal grooving of grain boundaries enlarging surface roughness (Mullins 1958)

novelty_claims.quote: Thus, the H2O effect has not been determined quantitatively.
As mentioned in the introduction, the CH2O exponent for Si diffusion in wadsleyite was not quantitatively determined previously.
[...] study, the H2O enhancement of Si diffusion in wadsleyite is quantitatively determined with a CH2O exponent of r = 0.8 ± 0.1

limits: No review file was supplied, so the review sequence is absent; the acknowledgment mentions two anonymous reviewers. Sub-claims hold different statuses. Near-isotropy is regularity_in_range: it holds at 1573–1873 K and 10–5,300 ppm, and an apparent factor of three is attributed to scatter. (2H)Si-controlled Si diffusion is best_explanation, and it depends on assuming the same mechanism in Fe-free and Fe-bearing wadsleyite. The viscosity reduction and the plume-shape account are best_explanation at most: they assume η ∝ 1/DSi, a temperature-independent r, an olivine-like pressure dependence and r ≈ 1.1 for ringwoodite, and are not tested against data beyond a qualitative match to cited seismic images. The Plain Language Summary gives more than 2.4 orders of magnitude weakening, while the main text gives 1.6 orders; the paper does not reconcile the two. One run temperature was estimated from a power-temperature relation. Duplicate craters on the same runs (Table 1) are not discussed as reproductions. The FTIR text repeats E//[100] three times, an apparent typo. Coding the Shimojuku comparison as a replication performed here is the coder's inference. Composition is none_fits: this is laboratory parameter estimation with set conditions, followed by an interpretive defect-chemistry comparison. No listed composition (strong inference, trace series, nature's repetition, etc.) describes it. The rival exclusion is secondary to the estimate. How crater locations were chosen beyond the topography criterion is not documented (inference).

disagreements.target: Shimojuku et al. (2004, 2009, 2010) Si diffusion coefficients in wadsleyite
disagreements.support: Absolute DSi in this study, adjusted to 1 wt. ppm H2O, matches Shimojuku's values at 10–140 ppm. The authors attribute the offset to polycrystalline samples, large topography, Si activity or temperature differences.
disagreements.quote: However, the absolute values of DSi in this study are higher (Figure 7)

disagreements.target: Shimojuku et al. (2004, 2009, 2010) polycrystalline SIMS method
disagreements.support: Polycrystals cannot resolve anisotropy and enlarge surface roughness, degrading SIMS depth resolution. Their 40–300 nm topography is comparable to their diffusion lengths.
disagreements.quote: [...] coefficients (Shimojuku et al., 2004, 2009, 2010) were obtained from polycrystalline samples, which does not allow to identify diffusion anisotropy.

disagreements.target: Hustoft et al. (2013) deformation experiments on H2O weakening
disagreements.support: The weakening is accepted, but its magnitude is not quantified because H2O contents in the open-system deformation samples were not controlled.
disagreements.quote: [...] in the samples were not well controlled, as they pointed out

disagreements.target: Shatskiy et al. (2010) reported Si diffusion anisotropy in stishovite
disagreements.support: The authors judge the reported anisotropy to lie within experimental uncertainty, consistent with isotropic Si diffusion in mantle minerals.
disagreements.quote: its magnitude of anisotropy is within experimental uncertainty as well
